section.title: Balaam and the Donkey
section.sectionRationale: This opens the Balaam cycle, a strange and important seam in Numbers where a foreign diviner, hired to curse Israel, is repeatedly overruled by the God of Israel, even through the mouth of his own donkey. It shows, before a single oracle is spoken, that no power on earth can curse what God has blessed.
section.thesis: Terrified of Israel's advance, Balak hires the diviner Balaam to curse them, but the LORD will not permit it, restraining Balaam through direct warning and then through his own donkey's eyes, until Balaam himself sees the angel of the LORD and is left with only one commission: to speak whatever God tells him.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Moab's fear of Israel and Balak's summons to Balaam; God's initial refusal and Balaam's second summons; the donkey who sees the angel of the LORD before Balaam does; and Balaam's arrival before Balak with a warning that he can only speak God's word.

verses.text: Then the Israelites traveled on and camped in the plains of Moab near the Jordan, across from Jericho.
Now Balak son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites,
and Moab was terrified of the people because they were numerous. Indeed, Moab dreaded the Israelites.
So the Moabites said to the elders of Midian, “This horde will devour everything around us, as an ox licks up the grass of the field.” Since Balak son of Zippor was king of Moab at that time,

he sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor at Pethor, which is by the Euphrates in the land of his people. “Behold, a people has come out of Egypt,” said Balak. “They cover the face of the land and have settled next to me.

So please come now and put a {{curse|curse}} on this people, because they are too mighty for me. Perhaps I may be able to defeat them and drive them out of the land; for I know that those you bless are blessed, and those you curse are cursed.”
The elders of Moab and Midian departed with the fees for divination in hand. They came to Balaam and relayed to him the words of Balak.
“Spend the night here,” Balaam replied, “and I will give you the answer that the LORD speaks to me.” So the princes of Moab stayed with Balaam.

units.label: God's first refusal and Balak's second summons
units.note: you are not to curse this people

verses.text: Then God came to Balaam and asked, “Who are these men with you?”
And Balaam said to God, “Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, sent me this message:
‘Behold, a people has come out of Egypt, and they cover the face of the land. Now come and put a curse on them for me. Perhaps I may be able to fight against them and drive them away.’”
But God said to Balaam, “Do not go with them. You are not to curse this people, for they are blessed.”
So Balaam got up the next morning and said to Balak's princes, “Go back to your homeland, because the LORD has refused to let me go with you.”
And the princes of Moab arose, returned to Balak, and said, “Balaam refused to come with us.”
Then Balak sent other princes, more numerous and more distinguished than the first messengers.
They came to Balaam and said, “This is what Balak son of Zippor says: ‘Please let nothing hinder you from coming to me,
for I will honor you richly and do whatever you say. So please come and put a curse on this people for me!’”
But Balaam replied to the servants of Balak, “If Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not do anything small or great to go beyond the command of the LORD my God.
So now, please stay here overnight as the others did, that I may find out what else the LORD has to tell me.”
That night God came to Balaam and said, “Since these men have come to summon you, get up and go with them, but you must only do what I tell you.”
So in the morning Balaam got up, saddled his donkey, and went with the princes of Moab.

units.label: The donkey sees the angel of the LORD
units.note: an angel with a drawn sword

media.alt: A donkey pressed against a wall before an unseen figure blocking the road
media.caption: The donkey sees the angel of the LORD before her rider does.

verses.text: Then God's anger was kindled because Balaam was going along, and the {{angel|angel of the LORD}} stood in the road to oppose him. Balaam was riding his donkey, and his two servants were with him.
When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand, she turned off the path and went into a field. So Balaam beat her to return her to the path.
Then the angel of the LORD stood in a narrow passage between two vineyards, with walls on either side.
And the donkey saw the angel of the LORD and pressed herself against the wall, crushing Balaam's foot against it. So he beat her once again.
And the angel of the LORD moved on ahead and stood in a narrow place where there was no room to turn to the right or left.
When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she lay down under Balaam, and he became furious and beat her with his staff.
Then the LORD opened the donkey's mouth, and she said to Balaam, “What have I done to you that you have beaten me these three times?”
Balaam answered the donkey, “You have made a fool of me! If I had a sword in my hand, I would kill you right now!”
But the donkey said to Balaam, “Am I not the donkey you have ridden all your life until today? Have I ever treated you this way before?” “No,” he replied.
Then the LORD opened Balaam's eyes, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand. And Balaam bowed low and fell facedown.
The angel of the LORD asked him, “Why have you beaten your donkey these three times? Behold, I have come out to oppose you, because your way is perverse before me.
The donkey saw me and turned away from me these three times. If she had not turned away, then by now I would surely have killed you and let her live.”
“I have sinned,” Balaam said to the angel of the LORD, “for I did not realize that you were standing in the road to confront me. And now, if this is displeasing in your sight, I will go back home.”
But the angel of the LORD said to Balaam, “Go with the men, but you are to speak only what I tell you.” So Balaam went with the princes of Balak.

units.label: Balaam arrives before Balak
units.note: only the word God puts in my mouth

verses.text: When Balak heard that Balaam was coming, he went out to meet him at the Moabite city on the Arnon border, at the edge of his territory.
And he said to Balaam, “Did I not send you an urgent summons? Why did you not come to me? Am I really not able to richly reward you?”
“See, I have come to you,” Balaam replied, “but can I say just anything? I must speak only the word that God puts in my mouth.”
So Balaam accompanied Balak, and they came to Kiriath-huzoth.
Balak sacrificed cattle and sheep, and he gave portions to Balaam and the princes who were with him.
The next morning, Balak took Balaam and brought him up to Bamoth-baal. From there he could see the outskirts of the camp of the people.

curse.gloss: To curse, to bind with a curse. Balak believed Balaam's arar could overpower nations, but the chapter shows repeatedly that no human curse can touch what God has already blessed, echoing the promise to Abraham that whoever curses him will be cursed, Genesis 12:3.

angel.gloss: The angel of the LORD, a figure who speaks with God's own authority throughout the Old Testament. Here he blocks the road with a drawn sword, seen first only by the donkey, showing that God's opposition to Balaam's errand was real and dangerous even while permitting the journey.

basic.context: Terrified of Israel's numbers and recent victories, Balak, king of Moab, hires a famous foreign diviner named Balaam to curse them. God repeatedly restrains Balaam, first by direct refusal, then dramatically through Balaam's own donkey, who sees the angel of the LORD blocking the road before Balaam does.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real historical episode involving a real pagan diviner whom God chose to use and restrain for His own purposes. Balaam is a genuinely mixed figure, a professional diviner for hire who nonetheless hears from the true God and, at least outwardly, insists he can only speak what God allows.
basic.originalLanguages: Balak trusts that Balaam's power to arar, curse, can overpower nations, exactly the kind of pagan confidence in cursing and blessing that the LORD had already answered when He promised Abraham that whoever curses him would themselves be cursed. The malak YHWH, the angel of the LORD, appears here with a drawn sword, a figure of real divine authority who blocks Balaam's path before Balaam can even see him.
basic.typology: The donkey seeing what her supposedly seeing rider cannot is a piece of narrative irony that highlights a recurring biblical pattern: God opens the eyes of the humble and unlikely while the powerful and self-assured remain blind, a pattern fulfilled when Jesus thanks the Father for hiding truth from the wise and revealing it to little children, Matthew 11:25.
basic.christ: While this chapter has no direct messianic prophecy of its own, it sets up the larger Balaam cycle in which God's sovereign protection of His blessed people, unable to be cursed by any human power, anticipates the New Testament's confidence that nothing can separate God's people from His love in Christ, Romans 8:38-39.
basic.god: God is sovereign over even a hired pagan diviner, permitting Balaam's journey while still restraining his mouth to speak only truth; He is also strikingly patient and even humorous, giving a donkey speech before He finally opens Balaam's own eyes to see what was blocking him all along.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 12:3 grounds the whole episode in God's promise that those who bless Abraham's descendants are blessed and those who curse them are cursed. 2 Peter 2:15-16 and Jude 11 both later condemn Balaam's greed, using his own donkey's rebuke as proof of how far he had strayed from wisdom. Numbers 31:16 later reveals Balaam's own hand in Israel's later sin at Peor, complicating any simple reading of his character here.
basic.oneStory: No hired power, human or spiritual, can curse what God has already blessed. This chapter's donkey who sees more clearly than her master becomes a small, almost comic picture of a truth carried through the whole Bible: God protects and directs His purposes even through unlikely and imperfect instruments, right up to His final, unshakeable blessing of His people in Christ.

context.literary:
Numbers 22 opens a new movement. Israel has stopped travelling. From 22:1 to the end of the book the people stay camped in the plains of Moab, and for three chapters they vanish from the foreground altogether. The camera moves to a hilltop where a king and a hired seer plot against them, and Israel does not know it is happening. The reader watches a battle fought over Israel's head, in which the only weapon is words.

The chapter is built in three movements that each turn on a pattern of three. Balak sends messengers twice, and Balaam consults God twice, verses 7 to 21. On the road, the angel blocks the way three times, each place narrower than the last: first a field with room to turn aside, verse 23, then a lane between vineyard walls, verse 24, then a place 'where there was no room to turn to the right or left,' verse 26. The donkey is beaten three times, and she uses the phrase 'these three times,' verse 28, which the angel repeats, verses 32 and 33. The oracles that follow will also come in threes, with Balak's anger rising each time.

The donkey episode, verses 22 to 35, is a story within the story, and it previews the whole Balaam cycle. The donkey is pushed three times to go where her master wants; three times she turns aside because she sees the angel; her master is furious. In chapters 23 and 24 Balaam will be pushed three times by Balak to curse; three times he turns aside to blessing because he has seen what God wants; and his master is furious, 24:10. Balaam is to Balak what the donkey was to Balaam.

The chapter is also full of irony about sight. Balak 'saw' what Israel had done, verse 2. Israel covers the 'eye' of the land, verse 5. The donkey 'saw' the angel three times, verses 23, 25 and 27. Balaam sees nothing until 'the LORD opened Balaam's eyes,' verse 31. The chapter ends with Balak taking Balaam up to where 'he could see the outskirts of the camp,' verse 41. Seeing, and who truly sees, is the thread that ties the whole cycle together.
context.historical:
Moab was Israel's kin. Genesis 19:37 traces the Moabites to Lot, Abraham's nephew, and Deuteronomy 2:9 records the LORD's command, 'Do not harass the Moabites,' because He had given them their land. Israel had no designs on Moab. Balak's terror, verse 3, is therefore misplaced; he is afraid of a people God had forbidden to attack him. Midian's elders appear beside Moab's, verses 4 and 7. The Midianites were a loose group of peoples ranging through the regions east and south of Moab, and they will return in the sin at Peor and in the war of Numbers 31.

Balaam comes from far away. Pethor lay 'by the Euphrates,' verse 5, and Deuteronomy 23:4 places it in Aram-naharaim, the region of upper Mesopotamia. It is often identified with Pitru, a town near the Euphrates named in Assyrian records. The journey from there to Moab is several hundred miles and would take weeks each way. Two embassies and Balaam's own journey imply that months passed while Israel sat, unaware, in the plains.

The practice Balak hires is well attested. Mesopotamia had professional diviners who read omens from animal organs and other signs, and cursing specialists who were paid to pronounce words believed to bind an enemy. The 'fees for divination' of verse 7 were the professional's wages. Balak's confidence, 'those you bless are blessed, and those you curse are cursed,' verse 6, voices what the ancient world believed about such men.

Balaam is not merely a biblical character. In 1967 excavators at Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan valley found a plaster inscription, dated to around the eighth century BC, that names 'Balaam son of Beor' as 'a seer of the gods' who receives a night vision and weeps at what he is shown. The text is fragmentary and its religion is thoroughly pagan, but it confirms that Balaam's name and reputation were remembered for centuries east of the Jordan, not far from the plains of Moab. The sacrifices at Kiriath-huzoth and the ascent to Bamoth-baal, verses 40 and 41, place the scene in a landscape of local shrines. Bamoth-baal, 'the high places of Baal,' later appears among the towns of Reuben, Joshua 13:17.
context.canonical:
Balaam's story is remembered across the whole Bible, and the memory becomes sharper over time. Deuteronomy 23:4-5 uses it to explain why Moabites were excluded from the assembly: they 'hired Balaam son of Beor from Pethor in Aram-naharaim to curse you,' yet 'the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because the LORD your God loves you.' Joshua 24:9-10 has God say, 'I would not listen to Balaam. So he blessed you again and again.' Nehemiah 13:2 repeats the verdict when the returned exiles read the law, and Micah 6:5 tells Israel to 'remember what Balak king of Moab counseled and what Balaam son of Beor answered,' as proof of the righteousness of the LORD.

Later texts reveal what chapter 22 only hints. Numbers 31:16 says the seduction at Peor came 'through the counsel of Balaam,' and Numbers 31:8 and Joshua 13:22 record that he was killed with the sword among the Midianites, still called 'the diviner.' The man who hoped to 'die the death of the righteous,' Numbers 23:10, died among Israel's enemies.

The New Testament takes up both his greed and his teaching. Peter describes false teachers who follow 'the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness,' and recalls that he 'was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech,' 2 Peter 2:15-16. Jude says the ungodly 'have rushed headlong into the error of Balaam,' Jude 1:11. The risen Christ warns the church in Pergamum against 'the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the Israelites,' Revelation 2:14. Chapter 22 is where that way began: on a road, with a donkey, and a man who wanted to go where God had said no.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wrote this chapter so that Israel would know what happened on the hills above them while they slept in the plains. They were in danger they could not see and were defended by a God they had not asked. The first hearers were to grasp that their security did not rest on their own vigilance but on the LORD's word spoken over them, 'they are blessed,' verse 12.

He also meant them to see how a man can speak correctly about God and still be moving the wrong way. Balaam says the right things: 'I could not do anything small or great to go beyond the command of the LORD my God,' verse 18. Yet he invites the second embassy to stay 'that I may find out what else the LORD has to tell me,' verse 19, when God had already said no. Israel was to learn that the question is not whether a man uses God's name but whether his heart is bent toward God's will or his own profit.

Finally, the donkey episode was meant to humble. A professional seer, whose trade was seeing what others could not, is shown up by an animal. Israel, who would soon be surrounded by the diviners and omens of Canaan, was taught that insight into the purposes of God is not a technique to be bought. It is given when the LORD opens eyes, verse 31, and He may open the mouth of a donkey before He opens the eyes of a prophet.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a pagan diviner consulting God; it does not commend the practice. The law forbids anyone in Israel who 'practices divination' or 'interprets omens,' Deuteronomy 18:10-12, and Joshua 13:22 still calls Balaam 'the diviner' at his death. That God spoke to Balaam no more approves divination than His speaking to Pharaoh approved Pharaoh.

Nor should the donkey's speech be taken as a pattern for how God usually guides. It is a single, deliberate sign, and 2 Peter 2:16 treats it as a rebuke, not a model.

What does carry forward is a warning about the heart. Peter and Jude use Balaam as a type of the religious person who knows God's words but loves 'the wages of wickedness,' 2 Peter 2:15. The lesson for believers is to take God's first answer as final and not keep asking in hope that God will change His mind to suit our desires.

debates.question: Was Balaam a true prophet of the LORD or a pagan diviner God merely used?

views.label: A genuine, if compromised, prophet
views.case: Balaam speaks with God, calls Him 'the LORD my God,' verse 18, receives words from Him, and later the Spirit of God comes upon him, Numbers 24:2. Peter calls him 'the prophet,' 2 Peter 2:16. On this view he was a real prophet whose greed ruined him.

views.label: A pagan diviner God overruled for His own ends
views.case: Scripture never calls him a prophet of the LORD in the Old Testament; Joshua 13:22 calls him 'the diviner.' He uses omens, Numbers 24:1, takes fees, verse 7, and later counsels Israel's seduction, Numbers 31:16. God spoke through him as He spoke through Caiaphas, John 11:49-52, without making him His servant.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that God controlled his mouth, and both agree his heart was wrong. The second fits the whole biblical witness better, but either way the chapter warns that spiritual gifting is no proof of a right heart, which is Jesus' own warning in Matthew 7:22-23.

debates.question: Why is God angry that Balaam goes, when He had just told him to go?

views.label: God's anger is at Balaam's motive
views.case: God permitted the journey only on condition, 'you must only do what I tell you,' verse 20. Balaam went eagerly, and the angel calls his way 'perverse,' verse 32. On this reading God allowed what Balaam wanted in order to expose what he was, and His anger was at the greed driving the journey, which 2 Peter 2:15 names.

views.label: Balaam should never have asked a second time
views.case: God's first answer, 'Do not go with them,' verse 12, was clear. By asking again, verse 19, Balaam signalled that he hoped God would change His mind. God gave him what he asked, much as He gave Israel meat in Numbers 11, and then confronted him on the way.

views.label: The narrative joins two perspectives
views.case: Some suggest the story sets permission and anger side by side without resolving them, to show that God's permissive will and His pleasure are not the same thing.

debates.bearing: The first two views belong together. God's permission was real but conditional, and His anger was at the heart that had pressed for it. The angel's final word, 'Go with the men, but you are to speak only what I tell you,' verse 35, restates the condition of verse 20, which shows the journey itself was not the problem but the spirit in which Balaam undertook it.

study.originalLanguages:
Balak's panic in verses 3 to 6 is voiced in the language of Exodus. Moab 'dreaded' the Israelites, using the verb quts, the very word of Exodus 1:12, where 'the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites.' Balak calls them 'too mighty for me,' atsum, verse 6, echoing Pharaoh's 'too numerous and too powerful for us,' Exodus 1:9, where the same word stands. Moab has become a second Egypt, and the reader knows how the first one ended.

Balak says Israel covers 'the face of the land,' verses 5 and 11. The Hebrew is literally 'the eye of the land,' the same idiom used of the locusts in Exodus 10:5, 'They will cover the face of the land so that no one can see it.' It is the first of many plays on eyes and sight in the Balaam cycle. The land is blinded by Israel; Balaam is blind to the angel; the LORD will open his eyes.

Balak uses two verbs for cursing. In verse 6 he asks Balaam to 'put a curse,' arar, the verb of solemn, binding curse used in Genesis 12:3, 'curse those who curse you.' In verses 11 and 17 he uses qabab, a word for cursing that recurs again and again through the Balaam chapters. The 'fees for divination' of verse 7 are qesamim, from qasam, the verb forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10, 'practices divination.' Balak is not hiring a priest but a professional of the forbidden arts.

In verses 22 and 32 the angel of the LORD stands 'to oppose' Balaam. The Hebrew is lesatan, 'as an adversary,' from the same noun that later becomes the name Satan. Here it is not a name. The word describes a role, and 1 Samuel 29:4 uses it of David as a potential 'adversary' in battle, while 1 Kings 11:14 says 'the LORD raised up against Solomon an adversary.' In this chapter the adversary is the angel of the LORD Himself, standing against a man set on evil. The one who opposes Balaam is God's messenger, not God's enemy.

The angel's charge in verse 32, 'your way is perverse before me,' turns on derekh, 'way' or 'road,' which runs through the whole scene: the angel stands 'in the road,' verses 22, 23 and 31, and the donkey turns 'off the path,' verse 23. Balaam's literal road and his moral way are the same thing. The BSB footnote offers 'reckless or contrary' for the verb behind 'perverse.' Peter will call this 'the way of Balaam,' 2 Peter 2:15.

The donkey's phrase 'these three times,' verse 28, uses regalim, literally 'feet' or 'footfalls,' rather than the usual word for times. The same unusual word appears in Exodus 23:14, 'Three times a year you are to celebrate a feast to Me,' of Israel's pilgrim journeys. The donkey counts her master's journey in footsteps.

Finally, verse 31 says 'the LORD opened Balaam's eyes,' using galah, to uncover or reveal. It is the verb of revelation, and in Numbers 24:4 and 16 Balaam will describe himself as one 'who bows down with eyes wide open,' literally with eyes uncovered, the same verb. His later claim to open eyes goes back to this roadside, where God had to uncover them for him, and where he 'bowed low and fell facedown,' verse 31.

typology.type: The donkey who sees what the seer cannot
typology.fulfillment: A beast of burden perceives the angel while the professional seer is blind, and the LORD opens her mouth before He opens Balaam's eyes. The pattern recurs in Isaiah 1:3, 'the donkey its master's manger, but Israel does not know,' and comes to fullness when Jesus praises the Father for hiding things 'from the wise and learned' and revealing them 'to little children,' Matthew 11:25, and says He came 'so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind,' John 9:39. The type is modest; the donkey is not a picture of Christ but of the humble to whom God reveals Himself, 1 Corinthians 1:27.

typology.type: The angel of the LORD with a drawn sword on the road
typology.fulfillment: The angel speaks in the first person as God's own voice, 'your way is perverse before me,' verse 32, and Balaam falls facedown before him, as Joshua will before the commander of the LORD's army with drawn sword, Joshua 5:13-15. Many Christian interpreters have seen in the angel of the LORD an appearance of the Son before His incarnation. That is an inference, not a New Testament statement, but the escalation is clear: the one who once stood in the road to oppose a false prophet now says 'I am the way,' John 14:6, and He will come with a sharp sword from His mouth to judge, Revelation 19:15.

typology.type: A blessing that cannot be cursed
typology.fulfillment: God's first word, 'You are not to curse this people, for they are blessed,' verse 12, rests on Genesis 12:3. Deuteronomy 23:5 says God 'turned the curse into a blessing' because He loves His people. In Christ the same security is given to all who belong to Him: 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' and 'Who will bring any charge against God's elect?' Romans 8:31-33. The escalation is that Israel was protected from Balaam's words; believers are protected from the curse of the law itself, which Christ bore, Galatians 3:13-14. The type falls short in that Israel was still judged at Peor; the believer's standing in Christ does not fall.

study.christ:
This chapter does not speak of Christ directly, but it lays the groundwork for everything the oracles will say about Him, and it points to Him in at least three ways.

First, it shows a people defended without their knowledge. Israel sleeps in the plains of Moab while a king and a seer plot on the heights. The people never see the angel with the sword, never hear Balaam's attempts, never pray about any of it. Their defence is entirely God's initiative. That is the shape of the gospel. Paul says God showed His love in that 'while we were still sinners, Christ died for us,' Romans 5:8, and that 'Christ Jesus, who died, and more than that was raised to life, is at the right hand of God, and He is interceding for us,' Romans 8:34. Believers are defended in the heavenly places by a Mediator whose work they cannot see.

Second, the chapter sets the angel of the LORD against the false prophet. The angel stands in the road as God's own adversary to a man who would curse God's people for money. In the Gospels, Jesus stands against false teachers who make gain out of religion. He drives the sellers from the temple, John 2:14-16, and warns that many will say 'did we not prophesy in Your name,' only to hear 'I never knew you,' Matthew 7:22-23. Peter's use of Balaam in 2 Peter 2 comes in a passage about false teachers who deny 'the Master who bought them,' 2 Peter 2:1. The way of Balaam is set against the way of the Master.

Third, the chapter prepares the reader for the oracles, and the oracles will lead to a King. Balak hired Balaam to see Israel and curse; God will make him see a star and a scepter, Numbers 24:17. The man whose eyes God had to open on the road will be made to say 'I see him, but not now.' The humbling on the road is what makes the later vision possible. The seer who could not see an angel standing in front of him will be shown a King far in the future.

There is also a quiet contrast worth noticing. Balaam rides a donkey on a journey to curse Israel for money, and God blocks the road. Centuries later another rider comes on a donkey, not for profit but in humility, and He comes not to curse but to bless and save: 'See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey,' Matthew 21:5, quoting Zechariah 9:9. The New Testament does not draw this line itself, so it is an echo rather than a declared type, but it shows the difference between the false prophet and the true King.

Caution matters here. The donkey is not a figure of Christ, and the angel's sword is not a picture of the cross. What the chapter gives is the certainty that God's people are held by His word of blessing against every hostile power, a certainty that reaches its fullness in Christ, in whom believers are blessed 'with every spiritual blessing,' Ephesians 1:3.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is that He cannot be hired. Balak's whole approach assumes that divine power can be bought and directed. He offers fees, verse 7, then honour and 'whatever you say,' verse 17, then Balaam's price. The LORD answers the first embassy with a flat refusal and the reason: 'for they are blessed,' verse 12. God's blessing is not a commodity. It rests on His own prior word, Genesis 12:3, and no one can bid against it.

He is sovereign over outsiders. God speaks to a Mesopotamian diviner by night, verses 9 and 20, and meets him on the road. He is not a tribal god confined to Israel's camp. He is 'the LORD, the God of Israel,' and He is also the God of Pethor and of Moab. The nations do not know Him, but He knows them, and He directs even their plots.

He asks questions He knows the answers to. 'Who are these men with you?' verse 9, is not a request for information, any more than 'Where are you?' was in Genesis 3:9. It invites Balaam to state plainly what he is being asked to do and so to hear how wrong it is.

He is patient and humbling at the same time. God could have killed Balaam on the road; the angel says so, verse 33. Instead He first uses the donkey, then speaks through her, then opens Balaam's eyes. The humiliation is part of the mercy. A proud man is shown that his animal sees more than he does, which is exactly the lesson Balaam needs before he stands before Balak.

He is present in wrath against evil purposes. The angel of the LORD with a drawn sword is not a sentimental figure. He stands 'to oppose,' verse 22, and he would have struck. God's defence of His people includes active opposition to those who would harm them.

The chapter also shows the difference between God's permission and God's pleasure. God tells Balaam to go, verse 20, and is angry that he goes, verse 22. This is not confusion in God. It shows that God may allow a person to follow a course his heart has chosen while still confronting him on the way. Psalm 81:12 describes the same judgment: 'So I gave them up to their stubborn hearts.'

Above all, God defends His people when they are unaware. Israel never knew. Deuteronomy 23:5 gives the reason: 'because the LORD your God loves you.' The protection of chapter 22 flows from love, not from Israel's merit or vigilance. For worship, this chapter calls believers to rest in the God who watches when they sleep. 'The Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep,' Psalm 121:4.

crossReferences.note: God's promise to Abraham, 'I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you,' is the foundation of God's answer in Numbers 22:12. Balak's belief that Balaam controls blessing and cursing, 22:6, collides with the prior word of God who already holds that power.

Pharaoh fears that Israel is 'too numerous and too powerful for us,' and the Egyptians 'came to dread' them. Balak uses the same words in Numbers 22:3 and 22:6. Moab repeats Egypt's fear and Egypt's scheme, and the reader is meant to expect the same outcome.

Moses explains the exclusion of Moab by this episode, and gives the reason God defended Israel: 'the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because the LORD your God loves you.' Numbers 22 shows what that love did while Israel was unaware.

In Joshua's covenant renewal God recalls, 'I would not listen to Balaam. So he blessed you again and again.' The Balaam story became part of Israel's core history of salvation, told alongside the exodus and the conquest as proof of the LORD's faithfulness.

God calls Israel to 'remember what Balak king of Moab counseled and what Balaam son of Beor answered' in order to 'acknowledge the righteousness of the LORD.' The prophet treats the episode as evidence in God's case against an ungrateful people who forgot how He had defended them.

Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword who is commander of the LORD's army, and falls facedown before him. The parallel with the angel of Numbers 22:31 is close: the drawn sword, the falling down, the one who stands in the way. God's armed messenger opposes Balaam and leads Joshua.

Peter names 'the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness,' and recalls the donkey 'that spoke with a man's voice and restrained the prophet's madness.' He takes the road of Numbers 22 as a picture of false teachers driven by greed.

Jude sets 'the error of Balaam' between the path of Cain and the rebellion of Korah. Each is a biblical example of a man who approached God on his own terms. Balaam's error, pressing God for permission in hope of reward, is the heart of Numbers 22:19.

The risen Christ warns Pergamum against 'the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the Israelites.' What began in Numbers 22 as an attempt to curse became, Numbers 31:16 reveals, a plan to seduce, which is the more dangerous attack on God's people.

Balaam is killed with the sword among the kings of Midian, and his counsel is named as the cause of the sin at Peor. The man who spoke of the sword in Numbers 22:29 dies by it, and the diviner who could not curse Israel succeeded, for a time, in corrupting them.

Jesus thanks the Father for hiding things 'from the wise and learned' and revealing them 'to little children.' The donkey who sees the angel while the famous seer is blind is an early picture of the same divine habit of humbling the proud and revealing to the lowly.

Elisha prays, 'O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see,' and his servant sees the hills full of chariots of fire. As with Balaam in Numbers 22:31, the spiritual reality was there all along; what was needed was for the LORD to open the eyes.

'The Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.' Numbers 22 shows the truth of the psalm in narrative: Israel is asleep in the plains while God stands in the road against the one sent to curse them.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 12:3 set the terms for the whole Bible: God would bless those who blessed Abraham and curse those who cursed him, and through him all families of the earth would be blessed. Numbers 22 is the first time a nation tries to test that promise by formal curse. Balak does exactly what the promise said could not succeed, and he does it with the best curser money could buy. The chapter answers the question every reader of Genesis might ask: what happens when someone actually tries?

It also answers the long fear of Exodus. A king fears Israel's numbers and plots against them, as Pharaoh did. Pharaoh's plot failed through plagues and the sea; Balak's fails through a donkey and a word. The God who delivered Israel from Egypt goes on delivering them when they no longer need to cross a sea.

What the chapter sets up is the blessing of chapters 23 and 24, and the darker turn of chapter 25. Balaam will be unable to curse, but he will find another way, and Israel will fall at Peor. God's word of blessing holds, but Israel's heart remains the danger. That tension runs through the rest of the Old Testament: the promise stands, and the people keep failing to live in it.

The story moves on toward a King. The oracles of chapter 24 will see a star from Jacob, and that line runs through David to Christ. In Christ the promise to Abraham is finally fulfilled for the nations: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' so that 'the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus,' Galatians 3:13-14. The curse that Balaam could not pronounce, Christ took upon Himself, and the blessing that Balaam could not reverse is given to all who believe.

The story ends in the new creation, where there is 'no longer any curse,' Revelation 22:3. Every Balak and every Balaam, every power that has plotted to curse the people of God, will have failed. The false prophet, whose way began on a road with a donkey, is judged, Revelation 19:20. The people once defended without knowing it will see the face of the One who defended them, Revelation 22:4, and know at last how often He stood in the road on their behalf.

quiz.q: Why did Balak, king of Moab, send messengers to Balaam?

options.text: To hire him to curse Israel, whom Moab feared as too numerous and mighty.
options.note: Verses 2 to 6 describe this fear and the request for a curse directly.

options.text: To ask Balaam to negotiate a peace treaty with Israel.
options.note: Balak sought a curse against Israel, not a peace negotiation.

options.text: To invite Balaam to join Moab's army as a military advisor.
options.note: Balaam was summoned specifically as a diviner to curse Israel, not as a military figure.

options.text: No reason is given for the summons.
options.note: Verses 5 to 6 state the reason plainly.

quiz.q: What did God tell Balaam the first time He spoke to him about Balak's request?

options.text: Not to go with the men and not to curse Israel, because they are blessed.
options.note: Verse 12 records this direct refusal from God.

options.text: To go immediately and curse Israel as requested.
options.note: God's initial answer was a clear refusal, not permission.

options.text: To wait a year before responding to Balak.
options.note: No such waiting period is mentioned; God's initial answer was an immediate no.

options.text: God gave no response at all.
options.note: Verse 12 records a clear and direct response.

quiz.q: What did Balaam's donkey do three times on the road, and why?

options.text: She turned aside, pressed against a wall, and lay down, because she saw the angel of the LORD blocking the way.
options.note: Verses 23 to 27 describe these three actions and their cause.

options.text: She refused to move at all from the very start of the journey.
options.note: The donkey did move initially; her resistance came only when she saw the angel blocking the road.

options.text: She was simply exhausted from the long journey.
options.note: The text attributes her behavior directly to seeing the angel of the LORD, not exhaustion.

options.text: No reason is given for her behavior.
options.note: Verses 23, 25, and 27 each explicitly state she saw the angel of the LORD.

quiz.q: What did the angel of the LORD tell Balaam when his eyes were finally opened?

options.text: That his way was perverse before Him and that the donkey had saved his life by turning aside.
options.note: Verses 32 to 33 record this rebuke directly.

options.text: That Balaam had done nothing wrong and should proceed exactly as planned.
options.note: The angel rebukes Balaam's way as perverse, not approving it without correction.

options.text: That Balaam should return home immediately and never see Balak.
options.note: The angel actually permits Balaam to continue, but only to speak what God tells him, verse 35.

options.text: The angel said nothing to Balaam.
options.note: Verses 32 to 35 record a substantial exchange between the angel and Balaam.

quiz.q: What condition did Balaam repeatedly place on his ability to speak for Balak?

options.text: He could only speak the word that God put in his mouth.
options.note: Verses 18, 20, 35, and 38 all repeat this same restriction.

options.text: He would speak whatever Balak paid him enough to say.
options.note: Balaam explicitly denies this, saying not even a house full of silver and gold could make him exceed God's word, verse 18.

options.text: He would speak only curses, never blessings.
options.note: The text places no such restriction; Balaam says only that he must speak what God gives him, whatever that turns out to be.

options.text: No condition is mentioned.
options.note: This condition is repeated explicitly at least four times in the chapter.

questions: Balak trusted that a hired curse could overpower God's blessing on Israel. What powers or opinions do you fear might undo what God has already secured for you?
Balaam's donkey saw the angel of the LORD before her supposedly perceptive rider did. Where might you be missing what God is doing because you trust your own insight too much?

Balaam kept insisting he could only speak what God gave him, yet later Scripture reveals a compromised heart underneath. Where might your outward compliance with God's word be covering a heart still bent on your own gain?
God restrained a hired diviner rather than leaving Israel's protection to chance. Where do you need to trust that God is guarding you in ways you cannot yet see?

The angel of the LORD stood in Balaam's way with a drawn sword before Balaam ever noticed danger. How does it change your prayer life to know God sometimes blocks a path you cannot yet see is dangerous?

translationNotes.note: Pethor by the Euphrates places Balaam's home far to the northeast, in Mesopotamia, underscoring that Balak sought out a renowned foreign diviner rather than a local one.

The angel of the LORD, malak YHWH, is a figure who elsewhere in the Old Testament speaks and acts with God's own authority; the phrase does not always distinguish sharply between the angel and God Himself in the narrative.

Some manuscripts and versions read Pethor as being by the river of the land of Amaw rather than simply of his people, a minor textual variation reflecting an otherwise unattested regional name; it does not affect the sense of the passage.
